pr_title: Fix command line parsing for ansible-vault encrypt_string --prompt
pr_body:
##### SUMMARY
At the moment executing `ansible-vault encrypt_string --prompt` won't work, throwing an error if an additional string isn't passed as an argument. This would result in two encrypted strings and thus isn't the intended behaviour.

This change corrects the conditions needed to trigger a read from stdin while retaining the original check to ensure that `--prompt` and stdin can't be used simultaneously.

The existing unit test has been modified to not require an additional string, and a new one has been created to verify an error is thrown if both `--prompt` and stdin are used.

Fixes #70200

##### ISSUE TYPE
- Bugfix Pull Request

##### COMPONENT NAME
ansible-vault

##### ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
N/A

My opinion is the `--prompt` argument has an issue and does not work the way most users would assume. It's confusing and unusable. It's also preventing secure vaulting of secrets by ensuring they don't end up in bash history or auditd exec logs for the `encrypt_string` sub-command. No addressing this prompt issue will drive the workaround of users including secrets as arguments that end up in unencrypted log files and is poor security practice.

I'm astonished that this issue is still open since there is a PR pending that would solve it!
Please merge it.
@zanna-37 the problem is that we don't all agree that the PR is the correct solution

Ok, can we have a discussion on possible solutions and their pros and cons?
Because I currently don't see how the flag `--prompt` can be used.

The logical expectation is that `ansible-vault encrypt_string --prompt` spawns a prompt that asks for an (optional) variable name and a value.
Now, to achieve the same result, I need to write  `ansible-vault encrypt_string --prompt ignore_me` which works, but also encrypts the useless value "ignore_me".

IMHO `--prompt` should not be available for `encrypt_string`. It was added before `encrypt_string` existed for the purpose of handling a file or full value. When `encrypt_string `was added no new code to handle 'prompting' was, hence the current state. 

I think it is trivial to add `varname: !vault |` to the output for use in an editor/etc, but that is just MY opinion ... why the ticket is still open. Aside from the issues with the submitted PR/solution.

Ok, then what would you suggest for encrypting a value without passing it in clear-text in the terminal, or with variables? Is there a way? Should we add a new command or flag?

I would like something similar to what `read -s` does (even if they are _very_ different). The vault should ask for an input without showing it, and give the output encrypted.
just use `encrypt` with prompt, the value is still the 'correct encrypted format', the only thing encrypt_string adds onto it is `varname: !vault |\n`

@bcoca 
But prompt is not available with encrypt. It will always ask for stdin which does not solve the problem that the password ends in your bash-history
good point, we should fix this then

For me this works

`ansible-vault encrypt_string --encrypt-vault-id dev --stdin-name 'DB_PASS'`

or simply

`ansible-vault encrypt_string --encrypt-vault-id dev --name 'DB_PASS'`

I still see no good way to generate an encrypted string from hidden input...  `ansible-vault encrypt` is for encrypting whole files. `ansible-vaul encrypt_string --stdin-name foo` is reading from stdin, therefore input is not hidden. Only way is using the form that was shown in the description above which generates two encrypted strings: `ansible-vault encrypt_string --prompt "test_string"`. :-/

I agree, the `--prompt` option is very confusing and the error you get when using it only makes the user even more confused. When passing that option, you're thinking that _you are_ telling `ansible-vault` _not_ to use stdin. That's the whole point. And there's no other option to explicitly disable stdin either, so there's no obvious way of understanding what the application wants you to do, or what combination of options accomplishes what you want.

At best, the errors and help text need to be rewritten for greater clarity. At worst, the application itself is actively working to confuse the user by giving blatantly contradictory errors and responses.

I also agree that there needs to be a way to easily pass strings to the application without displaying them clearly on the screen or, even worse, preserving them in the shell history. Even with the implicit prompt, the use is somewhat confusing and unclear, and may even vary between shells. For example:

```
$ ansible-vault encrypt_string
New Vault password:
Confirm New Vault password:
Reading plaintext input from stdin. (ctrl-d to end input)
foobar!vault |
          $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
          37393531613538323234303136373864633464646630333566646430623534306536316135396234
          3736616364356337326137356363636437333231396132630a353366663532343938343438363030
          32353962306561323362653830303232353363393539326139333233633665386433343732643239
          3261636134643331300a336663663038613339343662343865666462353235633961343133323739
          3662
Encryption successful
```

First of all, it's inconsistent. It takes in the encryption password properly, in invisible masked form, but then asks for the stdin input in clear, visible form. They're both secrets, they should both be treated like it.

Second of all, in Bash I have to press Ctrl+D _twice_, which is not explained anywhere. Pressing it just once, nothing happens. This is where I've had different experiences on different systems. Sometimes once is enough, sometimes it isn't. I'm not sure exactly what dictates this.

Third, the encrypted output is mixed with the plaintext input, without any separation or clear delineation. I'd have to take great care to select and copy exactly what makes up the encrypted part, without accidentally adding a character from the plaintext input, or the "Encryption successful" line afterwards. This is just unnecessary. Why the encrypted version can't be printed after one or two blank lines, properly and visibly separated from the input, is beyond me. This should be obvious, frankly.

For simple strings, wrapping ansible-vault with other bash or shell tools might work, like `read -p "secret: " -s secret; ansible-vault encrypt_string "$secret"`, but A) this leaves the sensitive, secret data hanging around in a variable, and B) this doesn't allow for multiline blocks of text, like SSH keys. It also shouldn't really be necessary, since the whole point of `ansible-vault encrypt_string` is to take in single- or multiline strings directly and encrypt them.

Please consider rethinking the way ansible-vault works along these lines, or _at the very least_, rewrite the errors and help text to more clearly explain how the tool should be used, and what the options available actually do.
